relations.note: Ratatoskr carries malicious speech between Níðhǫggr and the eagle.
Týr entered the flyting immediately after Njǫrðr’s exchange with Loki.
Sigurd descends from Óðinn through Sigi and the Völsung lineage.
Óðinn, disguised as an old man, helps Sigurd select Grani.
Óðinn, disguised as a one-eyed man, advises additional blood-drainage trenches.
Odin rides Sleipnir to Jötunheimr, Hel, and Ragnarök.
Disguised as Hárbarðr, Odin denies Thor passage and trades insults.

relations.myth: Ferryman’s contest of boasts and insults
relations.note: Odin, probably disguised as Hárbarðr, refuses Thor passage and frustrates him verbally.
Thor is repeatedly presented as Odin's son.
Wodan and Wigi-Þonar appear together, but their grammatical relationship is disputed.
One Snorrian formula calls Týr Odin's son, conflicting with Hymiskviða.
Tyr and Thor participate in an assembly where Ygg’s child confronts Ægir.
Ollerus impersonates and temporarily replaces exiled Othinus using a spell-marked bone.
Othinus returns to power and drives the usurping Ollerus away.
Odin's newborn son Váli fulfills the planned vengeance by killing Höðr.
Odin fathers Váli on Rindr to avenge Baldr.
Odin sends or directs valkyries to choose and serve the battle-slain.
Vidar avenges Odin’s death by attacking and killing Fenrir.
Vidar is consistently identified as Odin’s son.

relations.myth: The seat and cup at Ægir’s feast
relations.note: Vidar obeys Odin by yielding his seat and pouring Loki a drink.
Wotan is Wagner's transformed dramatic version of the Germanic god Odin.
Post-medieval Swedish and Danish folklore identifies supernatural hunts or passing companies with Odin.
Odin and his brothers fashion the cosmos from Ymir's body.
Odin and Borr's other sons kill Ymir.
Odin and his brothers kill Ymir before using his corpse.
Odin and his brothers transform Ymir's dismembered body into the world.
Alpine folklore connects Perchta with seasonal companies and dangerous Twelve-Night visitations.
Rán is Ægir’s wife and jointly mothers his wave-daughters.
They complain to Loge about the theft and ask him for help.
Wotan learns their grievance, refuses restitution, and dismisses their lament.
Poetic diction calls Þórr Sif’s intimate or husband; Snorri explicitly calls her his wife.
relations.source: Eysteinn Valdason; Hymiskviða; Þrymskviða; Snorri’s Edda

relations.note: Thor reacts furiously after Loki cuts Sif’s hair.
Snorri names Ullr as Sif’s son and Þórr’s stepson.
Siegfried impatiently answers the disguised Wotan’s riddles.
Siegfried breaks Wotan’s spear with Nothung during their confrontation.
Loki's son Váli is Sleipnir's maternal half-sibling in one genealogy.
Týr travels with Thor to obtain Hymir’s cauldron for Ægir.
Tyr reveals Hymir’s cauldron and accompanies Thor on the quest to retrieve it.
Ullr is Sif’s son and therefore Thor’s stepson by implication.
Snorri compares Vidar’s strength favorably with Thor’s.
Hymir pursues Thor after Thor carries away the immense brewing cauldron.
Hymir reluctantly fishes with Thor and reacts fearfully when Thor hooks the serpent.
Tyr calls Hymir his father, making him giant-descended in this genealogy.
Tyr approaches Hymir’s hall so the gods can obtain the giant’s cauldron.

relations.myth: The Norns recount history before their rope breaks
relations.note: Wagner portrays the three Norns as daughters or extensions of Erda’s wisdom.
Vidar and Váli jointly survive and inhabit the gods’ sanctuaries.
Snorri places Vidar and Váli together at Iðavöllr after Ragnarök.
Vidar and Váli are presented as brother survivors.
Wagner’s nine Walküren are Wotan’s daughters and supernatural battle-agents.
Wotan strips Brünnhilde’s divinity, puts her to sleep, and surrounds her with fire.
Wotan threatens the Valkyries when they shelter the disobedient Brünnhilde.
Wotan commands the Walküren to gather fallen heroes for his forces.
The Valkyries collect fallen heroes to form Wotan's army.
Fricka’s demand forces Wotan’s command against Siegmund, which Brünnhilde disobeys.
A swan-clad Valkyrie lives with Vǫlundr for years before departing.
Regional German traditions name Wodan or Wode as the supernatural hunter or leader.

Alecto.note: Old English glossary tradition uses wælcyrge to translate the Fury Alecto.

Alfrigg.note: Alfrigg demands a night with Freyja as his share of the necklace’s price.

Andhrímnir.note: Andhrímnir cooks Sæhrímnir for the einherjar.

Andvari.note: Wagner transferred Andvari’s cursed-ring and seized-treasure functions to Alberich.
Andvari.source: Wagner’s Ring and Old Norse sources

Andvari.note: Fáfnir takes possession of Andvari’s cursed gold without meeting him directly.
Loki captures Andvari and confiscates his treasure and ring.
Loki captures Andvari in fish form using the net borrowed from Rán.

Angeyja.note: Angeyja is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Angrboða.note: Snorri identifies Angrboða as Fenrir’s mother.
Angrboða bears Hel, Fenrir, and Jörmungandr with Loki.
Angrboða is named as Jǫrmungandr’s mother.
Snorri makes the giantess Angrboða Loki’s partner and mother of three children.

Ask.note: Odin and two companions animate the lifeless Ask.
Odin, Vili, and Vé give Ask life and human faculties.

Atla.note: Atla is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Atreus.note: The games reinvent Jǫrmungandr as a speaking giant allied with Atreus.

Auberon.note: Auberon is Alberich’s French cognate development, but has a distinct biography.

Aurboða.note: Aurboða is named as Gerðr’s mother.

Aurvandill.note: Thor carries Gróa’s husband Aurvandill in a basket out of giant-land.
Thor breaks off Aurvandill’s frozen toe and casts it skyward as a star.

Baugi.note: Odin deceives Baugi, works for him, and uses him to breach Hnitbjörg.

Beda.note: Beda jointly receives Roman-period altar dedications with Mars Thingsus, inferentially identified as Tyr.

Beli.note: Freyr kills the jǫtunn Beli with a hart antler.

Bergelmir.note: Aurgelmir is named as Bergelmir's grandfather through Þrúðgelmir.
Bergelmir and his wife escape the flood caused by Ymir's blood.

Berlingr.note: Berlingr demands a night with Freyja as his share of the necklace’s price.

Beyla.note: Beyla is identified as Freyr’s servant.
Beyla accompanies Freyr at Ægir’s feast and is insulted by Loki.

Blóðughadda.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Blóðughadda is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Borr.note: Búri begets Borr; Borr's mother and the reproductive mechanism are unrecorded.
Bestla is Borr's wife and bears his three sons.
The Jotunn Bestla marries Borr and bears three sons.
Odin is Borr's son alongside Vili and Vé.

Bous.note: Bous posthumously avenges Balderus by killing Høtherus.

Brokkr.note: Brokkr helps manufacture Gullinbursti, which the gods award to Freyr.
Loki wagers his head that Brokkr’s brother cannot equal Ívaldi’s sons’ treasures.
Fly-shaped Loki bites Brokkr repeatedly to sabotage his work at the bellows.
After Loki evades forfeiting his head, Brokkr sews Loki’s lips shut.
Brokkr helps manufacture and present Mjǫllnir to Thor during Loki’s wager.

Brünnhilde.note: Fricka presses the judgment that Brünnhilde must enforce against Siegmund.
They receive Brünnhilde’s news and carry it home to Wotan.
Wagner gives Wotan a central dramatic relationship with Brünnhilde.
They obey her command to recover and purify the ring from her ashes.
Siegfried passes the magic fire and awakens the former valkyrie.
Siegfried and Brünnhilde unite after he overcomes fear through love.

Byggvir.note: Byggvir is identified as Freyr’s servant.
Byggvir accompanies Freyr at Ægir’s feast and boasts of serving the gods.

Bylgja.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Bylgja is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Bára.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Bára replaces Drǫfn as Rán’s daughter in another list.

Bölþorn.note: Bestla is the daughter of the jötunn Bölþorn.

Búri.note: Auðhumla licks salty rime-stones for three days, gradually exposing Búri.
Borr is identified poetically as Búri's heir or descendant.
Búri emerges as Auðhumla nourishes Ymir in Ginnungagap.
Odin is Búri's grandson through Borr.

Býleistr.note: Snorri identifies Býleistr as Loki’s brother.

Daedalus.note: Scholars compare their peerless craft, royal detention, and flight from captivity.

Dagr.note: Nótt and Dellingr are the parents of Dagr.

Dellingr.note: The Jotunn-associated Nótt marries Dellingr and bears Dagr.

Donner.note: Donner hears or comments upon their lament during the gods’ ascent.
Wagner adapts the Germanic thunder god as the hammer-wielding Donner.
Wotan restrains Donner's contemplated force and enters Walhall with him.
Loge trades taunts and strategic advice with Donner.

Drǫfn.note: Drǫfn is Rán’s daughter in one variant of the nine-daughter list.

Dvalinn.note: Dvalinn demands a night with Freyja as his share of the necklace’s price.
Some norns are called daughters of Dvalinn and understood as dwarfish.

Dwarfs.note: Dwarfs first quicken like maggots within Ymir's dead flesh.

Dúfa.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Dúfa is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Egill.note: Völundr and Egill are brothers and co-dwellers in Wolfdales.
Egill gathers birds and helps Velent escape using constructed feathered wings.
Velent uses a blood-filled target so Egill's compelled shot appears successful.

Eistla.note: Eistla is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Eitri.note: Loki wagers that Eitri cannot forge treasures equal to those already obtained.

Eldir.note: Eldir serves Ægir and confronts Loki outside the feast hall.

Elli.note: Personified Old Age wrestles Thor and forces him onto one knee.

Embla.note: Odin and two companions animate the lifeless Embla.
Odin, Vili, and Vé give Embla life and human faculties.

Erichthonius.note: Grimm compares their lameness and extraordinary means of locomotion.

Eyrgjafa.note: Eyrgjafa is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Fafner.note: Alberich warns Fafner of danger while hoping to recover the ring.
Siegfried kills Fafner, a giant transformed into a dragon.

Fasolt.note: Wagner’s Fafner is the giant Fasolt’s brother.
Fafner kills Fasolt and takes the treasure paid to them.
Wagner reinvents giant-builder material through the giant Fasolt.
Fasolt builds Walhall for Wotan under a contract promising Freia.
Wotan pays Fasolt with Alberich's treasure after surrendering the Ring.

Fimafeng.note: Fimafeng serves Ægir efficiently at the feast before Loki kills him.
Loki kills Ægir’s servant after the gods praise the servants.

Fimmilena.note: Fimmilena jointly receives Roman-period altar dedications with Mars Thingsus, inferentially identified as Tyr.

Fjörgynn.note: Frigg is named Fjörgynn’s daughter; the parent’s identity and sex remain disputed.

Fjǫlnir.note: Fjǫlnir is Freyr’s son by Gerðr.
Gerðr and Freyr are made parents of the royal heir Fjǫlnir.

Forest Bird.note: The Forest Bird warns and guides Siegfried after he tastes dragon blood.

Forest maidens.note: Three supernatural women warn Hotherus about Balderus and advise his warfare.

Fornjótr.note: Late elemental genealogy makes Fornjótr the father of Hlér, identified as Ægir.

Fosite.note: Forseti is traditionally identified with Fosite, though the equation remains disputed.

Freia.note: Freia is pledged to Fafner and Fasolt as payment for Valhalla.
Freia hears or comments upon their lament during the gods’ ascent.
Wotan pledges Freia to the giants, then recovers her through the Ring.
Fricka protests Freia's surrender and welcomes her return.
Loge's proposal to ransom Freia with Alberich's gold enables her recovery.

Freki.note: Odin feeds Freki his meat while sustaining himself on wine.

Fricco.note: Adam’s Uppsala god Fricco is probably, but not certainly, identified with Freyr.

Froh.note: Wagner’s Froh is popularly associated with Freyr, but the equation is a modern adaptation.
Froh hears or comments upon their lament during the gods’ ascent.
Fricka and Froh together restrain Wotan from following Erda.
Wotan restrains Froh's contemplated force and enters Walhall with him.
Loge trades taunts and strategic advice with Froh.

Frø.note: Saxo’s euhemerized Uppsala ruler is connected with Freyr but cannot automatically be equated with him.

Fulla.note: Fulla is present when the gods receive Ægir at Ásgarðr.
Nanna sends Fulla a ring while Baldr returns Draupnir through Hermóðr.
Frigg sends Fulla ahead to warn Geirröðr about an approaching magician.
Fulla tends Frigg’s footwear, carries her chest, and knows her secrets.
Fulla and Gerðr are listed among the goddesses at Ægir’s feast.
Nanna sends Fulla a finger-ring from Hel through Hermóðr.
Hermóðr carries Nanna’s ring back for Fulla.
Volla participates in healing charms before Wodan successfully heals the horse.

Fárbauti.note: Snorri names Fárbauti as Loki’s father.

Gandalf.note: Tolkien partly shaped Gandalf from the Odinic wandering god archetype.

Gangr.note: Gangr is Þjazi’s brother and therefore Skaði’s paternal uncle.

Garm.note: Tyr fights the released hound Garm during Ragnarök.
Tyr kills Garm during their mutually fatal combat.
Garm kills Tyr during their mutually fatal combat.

Garmr.note: Garmr belongs to the forces opposing the einherjar and Æsir.

Gefjon.note: Odin sends Gefjon north to seek land, and she creates Zealand.

Gefjun.note: Gefjun appears as a guest in Ægir’s hall without direct exchange.
Gefjun and Gerðr are listed among the goddesses at Ægir’s feast.
Loki rebuffs Gefjun’s peacemaking and alleges she traded sex for jewelry.

Geirahǫð.note: Geirahǫð bears ale to the einherjar.

Geirrøðr.note: Captured by Geirrøðr, Loki promises to bring Þórr without his weapons.
Geirrøðr attempts to kill Thor with a heated iron projectile.
Thor catches the heated missile and throws it through Geirrøðr.

Gerhilde.note: Gerhilde is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Gerhilde joins the valkyrie gathering and dispute over sheltering Sieglinde.

Geri.note: Odin feeds Geri his meat while sustaining himself on wine.

Gersemi.note: Some Snorrian manuscripts name Gersemi as Freyja and Óðr’s daughter.

Gerðr.note: Gerðr is present at the banquet; the proposed daughter relationship is unestablished.
Gerðr becomes Freyr’s wife and bears Fjǫlnir in Snorri’s account.
Freyr desires Gerðr and sends Skírnir, whose coercive threats obtain her promised meeting.

Gjálp.note: Gjálp is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.
Gjálp tries to drown Thor by swelling Vimur; he checks the flood.

Gjálp.myth: The crushing chair at Geirrøðr’s hall
Gjálp.note: Thor breaks Gjálp’s back after she tries to crush him beneath his chair.

Gná.note: Gná conducts Frigg’s errands through different worlds.

Gorgons.note: Old English glosses associate wælcyrge with Gorgon-related classical terms.

Grafvǫlluðr.note: Grafvǫlluðr and Níðhǫggr are colocated beneath Yggdrasill without further interaction.

Grani.note: Grani is said to descend from Sleipnir, though intervening parentage is unstated.

Greip.note: Greip is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Greip.myth: The crushing chair at Geirrøðr’s hall
Greip.note: Greip helps raise Thor’s chair to crush him, but Thor breaks her back.

Grerr.note: Grerr demands a night with Freyja as his share of the necklace’s price.

Grimgerde.note: Grimgerde is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Grimgerde joins the valkyries during Brünnhilde's defiance of Wotan.

Grábakr.note: Grábakr and Níðhǫggr are colocated beneath Yggdrasill without further interaction.

Gríðr.note: Gríðr is named as Víðarr's mother by Odin.
Gríðr lends Thor her staff, iron gloves, and power-belt.
Snorri identifies the jötunn Gríðr as Vidar’s mother.

Gróa.note: Gróa chants healing spells to remove Hrungnir’s whetstone from Thor’s head.

Gudrun.note: Sigurd marries Gudrun after an enchanted drink erases his promises.

Gullfaxi.note: Sleipnir outruns Gullfaxi while Hrungnir pursues Óðinn into Ásgarðr.

Gullveig.note: Some modern scholars identify Freyja with Gullveig through gold, seiðr, and Vanir associations.

Gunnar.note: Sigurd exchanges forms with Gunnar and crosses Brynhild’s fire for him.

Gunnlöð.note: Odin spends three nights with Gunnlöð to obtain three drinks of mead.
Odin exploits Gunnlöð's trust, drains the mead, and abandons her.

Gunnr.myth: Skuld rides with valkyries to battle
Gunnr.note: Skuld rides with Gunnr and Róta to choose the slain and govern battles.

Gunther.note: Siegfried uses his invisibility cloak to help Gunther overcome Brünhild.

Guro Rysserova.note: Norwegian folklore makes Guro leader of the dangerous Christmas-season ride.

Gutthorm.note: Gutthorm mortally attacks Sigurd after Gunnar and Högni incite him.
The dying Sigurd throws Gram and cuts Gutthorm in two.

Guðmundr.note: Sinfjǫtli alleges that the einherjar fought over or because of Guðmundr.

Góinn.note: Góinn and Níðhǫggr are colocated beneath Yggdrasill without further interaction.

Göndul.note: Göndul helps select Hákon’s battle-death and escorts him toward the divine host.
Odin dispatches Göndul to choose slain warriors and escort royal dead.

Gǫll.note: Gǫll bears ale to the einherjar.

Hadingus.note: Dumézil interpreted Hadingus as a historicized transformation of Njǫrðr, based on closely parallel marriage motifs.

Hagen.note: Wagner makes Alberich Hagen’s father by Grimhilde.
Alberich visits Hagen and commands him to recover the ring.
Woglinde and Wellgunde seize Hagen and drag him beneath the Rhine.
Hagen spears Siegfried through his vulnerable spot during a hunt.

Hati.note: Hati is called the son of Hróðvitnir, identified with Fenrir.

Hefring.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Hefring is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Heiðr.note: Some scholars identify Freyja with Heiðr, though the dossier stresses substantial disagreement.

Heiðrún.note: Heiðrún supplies enough mead or ale for the einherjar’s hall.

Hela.note: Marvel reinvents Fenris as Hela’s enormous female wolf.

Helblindi.note: Snorri identifies Helblindi as Loki’s brother.

Helgi.note: Helgi leads a company from Valhǫll that a maid identifies as einherjar.

Helgi Haddingjaskati.note: Kára flies above Helgi in swan form and protects him magically during battle.
Helgi accidentally cuts off Kára’s leg, destroying her protective power.

Helgi Hjörvarðsson.note: Sváva gives the nameless prince his name and directs him toward a sword.
Sváva protects Helgi in battle and continues riding to battles after their betrothal.
Sváva becomes Helgi’s beloved after he requests her hand from her father.

Helgi Hundingsbani.note: Sigrún warns and supports Helgi against the marriage arranged with Hǫðbroddr.
Sigrún chooses and marries Helgi after the war against Hǫðbroddr.

Helmwige.note: Helmwige is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Helmwige joins the valkyries during Brünnhilde's defiance of Wotan.

Hercules.note: Scholars sometimes identify the Germanic Hercules with a Thor-like god, but evidence is indirect.

Herfjǫtur.note: Herfjǫtur bears ale to the einherjar.

Herlechin.note: The supernatural company bears Herlechin’s name, though his personal command is not narrated.

Hermóðr.note: Snorri classifies Hermóðr as Baldr’s brother.
Hermóðr seeks Baldr’s release and carries his gifts and messages home.

Hermóðr.myth: Hákon the Good’s reception in Valhǫll
Hermóðr.note: Hermóðr and Bragi jointly meet Hákon upon his arrival.
Hermóðr accompanies Bragi to greet Hákon at Óðinn’s command.
Frigg requests a rider and promises favor; Hermóðr accepts the mission.
Hermóðr asks Hel to release Baldr; she sets the universal-weeping test.
Loki as presumed Þökk indirectly defeats the release condition Hermóðr negotiated.
Manuscript wording calls Hermóðr Odin's boy or son.
Odin sends Hermóðr on Sleipnir to negotiate Baldr's release from Hel.
Sleipnir carries Hermóðr to Hel, leaps her gate, and returns with him.
Hermóðr joins Bragi in welcoming Hákon after the Valkyries select him.

Herne.note: Modern pagan representations place Herne at the Hunt’s head and conflate him with other horned figures.

Herodias.myth: Leadership of the nocturnal spirit company
Herodias.note: Canonistic and demonological traditions place Herodias and Holda within the same night-leader naming complex.
Herodias and Perchta appear together in a clerical catalogue without narrative interaction.
Medieval variants make Herodias mistress of a nocturnal supernatural company.

Hervör alvitr.note: She lives with Völundr for nine winters, then departs while he awaits her.

Heðinn.note: Hildr is represented as Heðinn’s abducted lover in the Hjaðningavíg tradition.

Hildisvíni.note: Freyja rides the boar Hildisvíni when visiting Hyndla.

Hildr.note: Hildr bears ale to the einherjar.

Himinglæva.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Himinglæva is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Himinhrjótr.note: Thor tears off Hymir’s great ox’s head and uses it as bait.

Hjördís.note: Hjördís gives birth to Sigurd after Sigmund’s death.

Hludana.note: Antiquarian and philological conjecture identifies inscribed Hludana as Holda's predecessor, but the equation remains unproven.

Hlín.note: Frigg commissions Hlín to protect people whom Frigg wishes to save.

Hlökk.note: Hlökk bears ale to the einherjar.

Hnoss.note: Hnoss is Freyja and Óðr’s daughter.

Horned God.myth: Modern Horned God leads the Hunt
Horned God.note: Twentieth-century neopagan representations sometimes make a universal Horned God the Hunt’s leader.

Hreiðmarr.note: Fáfnir kills his sleeping father and takes the entire hoard.
Loki obtains gold to satisfy Hreiðmarr’s ransom demand for Ótr’s death.

Hrist.note: Hrist bears drink in Valhǫll and is included among the hall’s serving valkyries.
Odin sends Hrist among the valkyries who choose or serve warriors.

Hrungnir.note: Freyja continues serving the drunken Hrungnir drink until Þórr arrives.
Hrungnir threatens to carry Freyja away after killing the gods.
Hrungnir admires Sleipnir and pursues him into Ásgarðr without fighting him.
Thor duels Hrungnir after the drunken giant threatens Ásgarðr and its goddesses.
Thor kills Hrungnir with Mjǫllnir but is wounded and pinned beneath him.

Hrímgrímnir.note: Skírnir threatens Gerðr with sexual subjection to the three-headed þurs Hrímgrímnir.

Hrǫnn.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Hrǫnn is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Hulk.note: Hulk fights Marvel’s reinvented Fenris Wolf.

Hyndla.note: Freyja coerces Hyndla into reciting Óttarr’s ancestry and yielding a memory drink.
Freyja threatens Hyndla with supernatural fire when she withholds the drink.

Hyrrokkin.note: Hyrrokkin is summoned and launches Hringhorni for Baldr’s funeral.

Hárbarðr.note: Hárbarðr tells Þórr that Sif has an unnamed lover at home.

Höðr.note: Höðr is Baldr’s brother in the canonical Icelandic genealogy.

Höðr.myth: Höðr kills Baldr with the fatal shoot
Höðr.note: Höðr shoots the plant weapon that kills Baldr.

Höðr.myth: Baldr and Höðr return after Ragnarök
Höðr.note: The former brothers and adversaries dwell together after the world’s renewal.
A Snorrian tradition makes the blind Höðr Odin's son.
Odin begets Váli, who kills Höðr for Baldr's death.
Saxo's Othinus opposes the human hero Høtherus after Balderus's death.
Vidar shares the renewed world with Höðr after Höðr returns.

Høtherus.note: Balderus and Høtherus wage war as rivals for Nanna.
Høtherus deliberately wounds Balderus with Mimingus’s supernatural sword.

Hœnir.note: Hœnir is present when the Æsir receive Ægir at Ásgarðr.
Hœnir is among the captured gods whose ransom later becomes Fáfnir’s hoard.
Hœnir is present when Þjazi forces Loki’s bargain concerning Iðunn.
Loki travels with Hœnir and Óðinn during their encounter with Þjazi.
Loki travels with Hœnir and Óðinn during the Ótr ransom episode.
Mímir serves as Hœnir’s counsellor and supplies judgments he cannot make alone.
Njǫrðr went to the Æsir while Hœnir was transferred reciprocally to the Vanir.
Odin and Hœnir help give life and faculties to the first humans.

Hǫðr.note: Loki places mistletoe in blind Hǫðr’s hand and aims the fatal shot.
Hǫðr is Váli’s paternal half-brother within Snorri’s genealogy.
Váli kills Hǫðr, identified as his brother Baldr’s killer.
In Saxo’s variant, Bous kills Hotherus in battle.

Ilmarinen.note: Modern comparative mythology juxtaposes the two master smiths without historical identification.

Imðr.note: Imðr is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Ing.note: Ing is comparatively identified with Yngvi-Freyr, though the poem does not state this.

Ivaldi.note: Iðunn is obscurely associated with Ivaldi’s children or lineage.

Iði.note: Iði is Þjazi’s brother and therefore Skaði’s paternal uncle.

Iðunn.note: Iðunn appears as a guest in Ægir’s hall without direct exchange.
Iðunn is consistently identified as Bragi’s wife.
Iðunn restrains Bragi during his escalating quarrel with Loki.
Iðunn and Freyr jointly attend Ægir’s feast without a direct exchange.
Iðunn and Gerðr are listed among the goddesses at Ægir’s feast.
Þjazi abducts Iðunn and her apples to Þrymheimr.
Loki lures Iðunn outside Ásgarðr so Þjazi can abduct her.
Loki transforms Iðunn into a nut and carries her home.
Loki insults Iðunn and alleges she embraced her brother’s killer.

Jarl.note: As Rígr, Heimdall fathers and later recognizes Jarl as his son.
As Rígr, Heimdall teaches Jarl runes and encourages conquest.

Járnsaxa.note: Járnsaxa is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.
Thor has a sexual relationship with Járnsaxa, who bears their son Magni.

Jörð.note: Jörð is Odin's partner and Thor's mother in genealogical formulas.
Jörð is a major analogue for Erda, though Erda is not simply Jörð renamed.

Jǫrð.note: Poetry repeatedly identifies Thor as the son of the personified Earth.

Karl.note: As Rígr, Heimdall fathers Karl, ancestor of farmers and craftsmen.

Konr ungr.note: Under the Rígr identification, Heimdall is ancestor of Jarl’s youngest son.

Kratos.note: The games reinvent Jǫrmungandr as a speaking giant allied with Kratos.
At Mimir’s request, Kratos decapitates him and later carries his reanimated head.

Kriemhild.note: Alberich recognizes Kriemhild’s claim and helps release the treasure for transport.
Siegfried marries Kriemhild in the continental tradition.
Seyfrid rescues Kriemhild during his expanded dragon adventures.

Kvasir.note: The two wisest hostages travel in opposite directions without a narrated meeting.
Odin steals the poetic mead made from Kvasir's blood.

Kári.note: Late elemental genealogy makes the wind-being Kári Ægir’s brother.

Kólga.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Kólga is named as a daughter of Rán and Ægir.

Laufey.note: Snorri names Laufey, also called Nál, as Loki’s mother.

Litr.note: Thor kicks the dwarf Litr into Baldr’s funeral fire, where he burns.

Lofn.note: Frigg or Odin authorizes Lofn to arrange otherwise obstructed unions.

Logi.note: Late elemental genealogy makes the fire-being Logi Ægir’s brother.
Loki loses an eating contest to Logi, the personification of wildfire.

Lussi.note: Scandinavian Christmas folklore gives Lussi command of a threatening nocturnal company.

Lóðurr.note: Modern scholars dispute identifying Loki with Lóðurr; no source states the equation.
Odin and Lóðurr help give life and faculties to the first humans.

Magni.note: Járnsaxa, or an unnamed giantess in the account, is Magni's mother.
Magni is Thor’s son by Járnsaxa.
The infant Magni frees Thor by lifting Hrungnir’s leg from him.
Thor rewards Magni with Hrungnir’s horse Gullfaxi.
Váli and Magni appear in the same post-Ragnarǫk prophecy without interacting directly.
Magni joins Vidar and the other survivors in the renewed world.

Meili.note: Meili is called Odin's son in Þórsdrápa.

Menglǫð.note: Comparative reconstructions sometimes identify Menglǫð with Freyja without textual attestation.

Mime.note: Alberich forces Mime to forge the Tarnhelm under threats and violence.
Alberich and Mime quarrel over the expected recovery of the ring.
Siegfried kills Mime after learning that Mime intends to murder him.

Mimingus.note: Hotherus coerces Mimingus into surrendering an invincible sword and magical bracelet.

Mist.note: Mist bears drink in Valhǫll and is included among the hall’s serving valkyries.
Odin sends Mist among the valkyries who choose or serve warriors.

Mithothyn.note: The false god Mithothyn seizes Odin's power and changes sacrificial practice.
Othinus returns, forcing the usurper Mithothyn to flee.

Mímr’s sons.note: The poem names Mímr’s sons but gives neither their number nor identities.

Móinn.note: Móinn and Níðhǫggr are colocated beneath Yggdrasill without further interaction.

Móðguðr.note: Móðguðr questions Hermóðr and directs him toward Hel.
Móðguðr questions Sleipnir's rider and remarks upon their unusually loud crossing.

Móði.note: Móði is Thor’s son, though his mother is unnamed.
Váli and Móði appear in the same post-Ragnarǫk prophecy without interacting directly.
Móði joins Vidar and the other survivors in the renewed world.

Narfi.note: A difficult early poetic genealogy calls Hel Narfi’s sister.
Narfi or Nari is Loki’s son; sources conflict over his punishment.
Narfi or Nari is Sleipnir's maternal half-sibling in differing Loki genealogies.

Nep.note: Forseti is Nep’s grandson through his mother Nanna.

Nibelung.note: Alberich is associated with Nibelung’s inherited treasure and defends it.

Njörðr.note: Skaði chooses Njörðr by his feet; incompatible homes separate them.
Odin leads the Æsir against Njörðr's Vanir before hostages are exchanged.
After peace, Njörðr joins Odin's Æsir as an exchanged hostage.

Njǫrðr.note: Njǫrðr appears as Ægir’s guest; the texts never identify them.
Njǫrðr is Freyja’s father in the standard genealogy.
Njǫrðr defends Freyja after Loki attacks her sexuality.
Njǫrðr sends Skírnir to discover the cause of Freyr’s distress.
Njǫrðr and Gerðr appear as guests in Ægir’s feast-frame.
Loki and Njǫrðr trade allegations about hostage status and sexual degradation.
Njǫrðr and Mímir travel on opposing sides of the hostage exchange.
Modern philology often treats Nerthus as an earlier form of Njǫrðr.
A reconstruction identifies Nerthus as Njǫrðr’s unnamed sister.
A reconstruction identifies Nerthus as Njǫrðr’s unnamed sister-wife.

Njǫrðr.myth: Choosing a husband by his feet
Njǫrðr.note: Skaði expects Baldr but selects Njǫrðr by viewing only the gods’ feet.
Their nine-night alternation fails because each detests the other’s dwelling.
Skaði cannot love Njǫrðr and, in Snorri’s variant, refuses relations.

Norns.note: Skuld appears among both Norns and battle-riding Valkyries, demonstrating categorical overlap.

Níðhöggr.note: Ratatoskr carries the eagle’s words downward to Níðhöggr.
Ratatoskr carries malicious words between Níðhöggr and the eagle.

Ortlinde.note: Ortlinde is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Ortlinde joins Brünnhilde during the valkyries' gathering and confrontation.

Ortnit.note: Alberich reveals that he is Ortnit’s supernatural dwarf father.
Alberich wrestles Ortnit before revealing their father-son relationship.
Alberich equips, counsels, conceals, and fights beside Ortnit during his bride quest.
Alberich supplies or directs Ortnit to marvelous weapons and armor.
Alberich warns Ortnit about the dragons and the danger of sleeping.

Othinus.note: Othinus fights for Balderus and later fathers the avenger Bous.

Phol.note: Phol rides with Wodan before Balder’s foal is injured; Phol’s identity is disputed.
Phol rides into the wood with Wodan before Balder's horse is injured.

Pyrrhus.note: Snorri equates Fenrir with Achilles’ son Pyrrhus.

Randgríðr.note: Randgríðr bears ale to the einherjar.

Regin.note: Regin fosters Sigurd, reforges Gram, and directs him against Fáfnir.
After hearing the birds’ warning, Sigurd decapitates Regin.

Reginleif.note: Reginleif bears ale to the einherjar.

Reginn.note: Fáfnir refuses Reginn a share; Reginn subsequently engineers Fáfnir’s death.
Reginn is the heroic smith Mímir’s brother; identity with Eddic Mímir is disputed.

Rindr.note: Rindr bears Odin's avenging son Váli.
Othinus uses disguises and magic during his coercive pursuit of Rinda.
Othinus magically incapacitates and coercively impregnates Rinda to beget Bous.
Rindr bears Váli in the western halls.
In Saxo’s variant, Bous is born to the Ruthenian princess Rinda.

Rossweisse.note: Rossweisse is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Rossweisse joins the valkyries during Brünnhilde's defiance of Wotan.

Ráðgríðr.note: Ráðgríðr bears ale to the einherjar.

Róta.myth: Skuld rides with valkyries to battle
Róta.note: Skuld rides with Róta and Gunnr to choose the slain and govern battles.

Rǫskva.note: Rǫskva becomes Thor’s servant as compensation after the goat-bone incident.

Santa Muerte.note: Modern devotional syncretism associates Hel with Santa Muerte.

Schilbung.note: Alberich is associated with Schilbung’s inherited treasure and defends it.

Schwertleite.note: Schwertleite is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Schwertleite joins the valkyries during Brünnhilde's defiance of Wotan.

Siegelind.note: Siegfried is the son of Queen Siegelind of Xanten.

Siegfried.note: Alberich attacks Siegfried after the Nibelung princes and their warriors are killed.
Defeated Alberich swears service and guards the hoard for Siegfried.
Siegfried takes Alberich’s invisibility garment after overcoming him.
Wagner’s Siegfried kills the dragon-transformed Fafner.
They request his ring and warn that retaining it will kill him that day.
They praise his apparent generosity, then condemn his obstinacy when he refuses.
Wotan is Siegfried's maternal grandfather through Sieglinde.
Wotan blocks Siegfried's path, but Siegfried breaks his spear with Nothung.

Sieglinde.note: Wotan fathers Sieglinde with an unnamed mortal woman.

Siegmund.note: Siegfried is the son of King Siegmund of Xanten.
Brünnhilde chooses to protect Siegmund after understanding Wotan’s suppressed desire.
Wotan fathers Siegmund with an unnamed mortal woman.

Siegmund.myth: Wotan attempts to create a free hero
Siegmund.note: Wotan fathers, arms, and protects Siegmund as his intended independent agent.
Fricka secures withdrawal of Wotan's protection, ensuring Siegmund's defeat.

Siegrune.note: Siegrune is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters.
Siegrune joins the valkyries during Brünnhilde's defiance of Wotan.

Sigi.note: Sigurd descends through Völsung from Óðinn’s son Sigi.

Sigmund.note: Sigurd is the posthumous son of Sigmund and Hjördís.

Sigmundr.note: Sigmundr is an einheri ordered to rise and greet the approaching Eiríkr.
Hermóðr receives armor while Sigmundr receives a sword in parallel.

Sigrún.note: Sigrún protects Helgi’s fleet as it escapes Rán’s grasp.

Sigurd Svein.note: Sigurd accompanies Guro in Norwegian traditions of the nocturnal company.

Sigurðr.note: The heroic Mímir is Sigurðr’s smith-master or foster-father; identity with Eddic Mímir is disputed.
Sigurðr cuts away the sleeper’s armor and awakens Sigrdrífa or Brynhildr.
The awakened Valkyrie teaches Sigurðr magical runes, ritual knowledge, and ethical counsel.
Sigurðr assumes Gunnarr’s shape, wins Brynhildr, and conceals his identity.

Sigurðr Fáfnisbani.note: Sigurðr hides beneath Fáfnir’s path and stabs him with Gram.
The dying Fáfnir questions Sigurðr and exchanges warnings and cosmological knowledge.

Sigyn.note: Sigyn is present when the gods receive Ægir at Ásgarðr.
Sigyn and Gerðr are listed among the goddesses at Ægir’s feast.
Sigyn is Loki’s wife and the mother or presumed mother of his sons.
Sigyn loyally catches the serpent’s venom above her bound husband.
Skaði installs the serpent while Sigyn catches its dripping venom.

Sindri.note: Sindri manufactures Gullinbursti with Brokkr, and the boar is awarded to Freyr.
Sindri manufactures and presents Mjǫllnir to Thor during Loki’s wager.

Sinfjǫtli.note: Sinfjǫtli is an einheri ordered to rise and greet the approaching Eiríkr.

Sinmara.note: A corrupt, editorially emended passage may associate Sinmara with Surtr as his consort.

Sinthgunt.note: Sinthgunt chants over Balder’s injured foal in the disputed continental episode.
Sinthgunt attempts a healing charm before Wodan heals Balder's horse.

Skaði.note: Skaði appears as a guest in Ægir’s hall without direct exchange.
Skaði is Freyr’s stepmother through her marriage to Njǫrðr.
Skaði urges Skírnir to question Freyr, whom she calls our son.
Skaði’s inquiry into Freyr’s distress leads to Skírnir’s embassy; she never meets Gerðr.
Gerðr is remotely related to Skaði through Þjazi’s unspecified kinship.
Skaði predicts Loki’s binding; Loki boasts about Þjazi and alleges intimacy with her.
Skaði suspends a venomous serpent above bound Loki.
Loki ties his genitals to a goat’s beard and makes Skaði laugh.
Skaði selected Njǫrðr as husband by his beautiful feet while expecting Baldr.
They alternated between mountain and seaside homes but separated because neither tolerated the other’s environment.

Skeggjǫld.note: Skeggjǫld bears ale to the einherjar.

Skírnir.note: Skírnir obtains the fetter Gleipnir from the dwarfs for Fenrir’s binding.
Skírnir serves as Freyr’s messenger, coercing Gerðr’s assent and reporting her meeting date.
Freyr gives Skírnir his horse and self-fighting sword for the journey.
Skírnir offers gifts, threatens Gerðr, invokes runic coercion, and negotiates the Barri meeting.
Skírnir forces Gerðr's agreement through violent and magical threats.

Skögul.note: Odin dispatches Skögul to choose slain warriors and escort royal dead.

Sköll.note: Sköll’s sonship is inferred from Fenrir’s brood, not explicitly stated.

Skǫgul.note: Skǫgul announces Hákon’s coming to Óðinn, enabling his reception among the einherjar.
Skǫgul bears ale to the einherjar.

Slagfiðr.note: Völundr and Slagfiðr are brothers and co-dwellers in Wolfdales.

Sons of Múspell.note: Surtr rides foremost among the sons of Múspell and leads their battle-host.

Sons of Ívaldi.note: The supernatural craftsmen make the magical ship Skíðblaðnir for Freyr.
The sons of Ívaldi manufacture golden replacement hair intended for Sif through Loki.

Sunna.note: Sunna joins her sister Sinthgunt in chanting over Balder’s foal.
Sunna attempts a healing charm before Wodan heals Balder's horse.

Suttungr.note: Odin enters Suttungr's mountain and steals his guarded poetic mead.

Suttungr.myth: Eagle pursuit after the mead theft
Suttungr.note: Suttungr pursues the fleeing Odin after both transform into eagles.

Svaðilfari.note: Svaðilfari performs the builder's extraordinary hauling work.
Mare-shaped Loki mates with Svaðilfari and subsequently bears Sleipnir.
Loki becomes a mare and lures Svaðilfari away, preventing the fortification’s completion.

Svaðilfari.myth: Birth during the fortification of Ásgarðr
Svaðilfari.note: The builder's supernatural stallion fathers Sleipnir with Loki in mare form.

Sváfnir.note: Sváfnir and Níðhǫggr are colocated beneath Yggdrasill without further interaction.

Sága.note: Odin and Sága drink daily together at Sökkvabekkr.

Sæhrímnir.note: Sæhrímnir is cooked as food for the einherjar and restored each evening in Snorri.

Sæmingr.note: Skaði and Óðinn are named as Sæmingr’s parents.

Sól.note: Fenrir attacks or takes Sól before her daughter replaces her.

Tanngnjóstr.myth: Thor’s goats at the farmer’s house
Tanngnjóstr.note: Thor kills and cooks his goat, preserving its bones for resurrection.
Thor restores his slaughtered goat to life with Mjǫllnir.

Tanngrisnir.myth: Thor’s goats at the farmer’s house
Tanngrisnir.note: Thor kills and cooks his goat, preserving its bones for resurrection.
Thor restores his slaughtered goat to life, though one goat remains lame.

Terra Mater.note: Tacitus equates or translates Nerthus as the Roman Mother Earth.

The unnamed eagle on Yggdrasil.note: Ratatoskr carries the eagle’s words downward to Níðhöggr.
Ratatoskr carries malicious words between the eagle and Níðhöggr.

Three Sisters.note: Perchta is counted among three unnamed sisters who receive food offerings.

Tisiphone.note: An Old English gloss uses wælcyrge as a learned equivalent for Tisiphone.

Tubal-cain.note: Traditional Witchcraft and related currents associate Wayland with Tubal-cain.

Unnamed mountain dwarfs.note: Two mountain dwarfs train Velent in their superior craft.
Velent kills the dwarfs before they can kill him.

Utgarthilocus.note: Saxo’s bound being is sometimes equated with Loki, but the identification remains uncertain.

Uðr.note: She is one of Ægir and Rán’s nine wave-daughters.
Uðr, also written Unnr, is named as Rán and Ægir’s daughter.

Vafþrúðnir.note: Disguised as Gagnráðr, Odin defeats Vafþrúðnir with an unanswerable question.
Odin's victory in the wager dooms or kills the giant.

Vanir.note: Njǫrðr originated among the Vanir and is consistently identified as one of them.
Njǫrðr will return home among the Vanir at the world’s end.

Vaði.note: Velent is Vaði's son in the prose-saga genealogy.
Vaði arranges Velent's apprenticeships and carries him across water.

Vili.note: Borr is the father of Vili, one of his three sons.
Bestla is the mother of Vili, one of her three sons.
Loki accuses Frigg of having embraced Vili during Odin’s absence.
Vili takes Frigg as wife when the Æsir believe Odin will not return.
Vili joins Óðinn and Vé in killing Ymir.
Vili is Odin's brother and a fellow son of Borr and Bestla.

Vili.myth: Slaying Ymir and creating the cosmos
Vili.note: Odin, Vili, and Vé kill Ymir and fashion the world.
Vili joins Odin and Vé in killing Ymir.
Vili and his brothers transform Ymir's dismembered body into the world.

Virgin Mary.note: Lady Holda is called Queen of Heaven, possibly reflecting Marian syncretism or clerical interpretation.

Viðarr.note: At Óðinn’s order, Viðarr gives Loki a seat and drink.

Viðga.note: Velent fathers Viðga, who inherits heroic equipment and joins the Dietrich cycle.

Volla.note: Volla joins her sister Frija in attempting to heal Balder’s foal.
The charm explicitly calls Friia and Volla sisters.
Friia and her sister Volla jointly participate in the healing charm.

Vé.note: Borr is the father of Vé, one of his three sons.
Bestla is the mother of Vé, one of her three sons.
Loki accuses Frigg of having embraced Vé during Odin’s absence.
Vé takes Frigg as wife when the Æsir believe Odin will not return.
Vé joins Óðinn and Vili in killing Ymir.
Vé is Odin's brother and a fellow son of Borr and Bestla.

Vé.myth: Slaying Ymir and creating the cosmos
Vé.note: Odin, Vili, and Vé kill Ymir and fashion the world.
Vé joins Odin and Vili in killing Ymir.
Vé and his brothers transform Ymir's dismembered body into the world.

Víðarr.note: Víðarr appears as a guest in Ægir’s hall without direct exchange.
Víðarr attacks Fenrir immediately after Odin’s death.
Víðarr kills Fenrir with a sword in the conventional poetic reading.
Víðarr tears Fenrir’s jaws apart and kills him.
Víðarr and Freyr jointly attend Ægir’s feast without a direct exchange.
Víðarr and Gerðr appear as guests in Ægir’s feast-frame.
Víðarr kills Fenrir in vengeance for Óðinn.
Later genealogy identifies Gríðr as Víðarr's mother.
Víðarr is Odin's silent son by Gríðr.
After Fenrir kills Odin, Víðarr avenges him by killing the wolf.
Váli and Víðarr survive and inhabit the gods’ sanctuaries after Surtr’s fire.

Waltraute.note: Waltraute is one of Brünnhilde's valkyrie sisters in Wagner's cycle.
Waltraute joins Brünnhilde and the valkyries during Wotan's confrontation.
Waltraute begs her to return the ring; Brünnhilde refuses.

Wodan.note: Wodan successfully chants a healing formula over Balder’s injured foal.

Yggdrasill.note: Iðunn is associated with a fall or descent from Yggdrasill.

Yngling royal dynasty.note: Freyr is presented as the divine ancestor of the Yngling royal dynasty.

dísir.note: Some Valkyries belong to the broader category of dísir, though the terms are not synonyms.

elves.note: Iðunn is obscurely connected with elves or an elvish lineage.
Some norns are described as being of elvish origin.

sons of Ívaldi.note: Loki commissions them to make Sif’s hair, Skíðblaðnir, and Gungnir.

the Horned God.note: Some modern witchcraft currents identify Wayland as a form or title of the Horned God.

the Moirai.note: Post-medieval comparison equated the Norns iconographically with the Greek Fates.

the Norns.myth: Mimir and Balder consult the Norns
the Norns.note: Mímir seeks knowledge from the Norns in a Romantic scene absent from medieval myth.
Erda is named mother of the three Norns.
Erda is presented as the source of the Norns' primordial knowledge.

the Parcae.note: Antiquaries translated nornir as Parcae, encouraging Classical identification.

the Vanir.note: The Vanir accuse the Æsir of fraud, behead Mímir, and return his head.
Odin leads the Æsir host in war against the Vanir.
The Æsir and Vanir make peace and exchange hostages.

the dead seeress.note: Odin compels a dead seeress from her grave with spells.
Odin questions the seeress until she recognizes and dismisses him.

the gods in Walhall.note: Loge privately considers consuming the assembled gods with fire.

the rime-giants.note: All giant-kind descend from the primordial giant Aurgelmir.

the serpent.note: Woden strikes a serpent with nine glory-twigs, breaking it into pieces.

the sons of Muspell.note: The sons of Muspell form part of the host opposing the einherjar.

the unnamed völva.note: Odin gives the völva rings and necklaces for prophecy or narration.
The völva recounts cosmic history and Ragnarök in response to Odin.

the unnamed “father”.note: The sisters call themselves daughters of a father associated with the Rhine.
Their father entrusts the gold to them and warns them about its power.

the Æsir.note: The Æsir throw weapons and stones at Baldr after Frigg’s oaths protect him.
The gods mourn Baldr, accompany his corpse, and arrange his ship-funeral.
The Æsir promise release if Fenrir fails, then break their pledge.
The Æsir bind, gag, and anchor Fenrir until Ragnarök.
The gods challenge Fenrir to test his strength against successive fetters.
Heimdall guards the gods’ sanctuary and warns the Æsir at Ragnarök.
The Æsir send Hermóðr, and Hel sets terms for Baldr’s return.
The Æsir discover that Rán possesses a net used to catch seafarers.
Tyr joins the Æsir in binding Fenrir and alone accepts the physical pledge.
Some norns are described as originating from or descending from the Æsir.
A learned poetic formula calls Vidar brother of the Æsir.
Vidar is characterized as the gods’ reserve support and avenger.

werewolves.myth: Nocturnal ride with Diana and werewolves
werewolves.note: Perchta rides nocturnally in a company that includes werewolves.

Áslaug.note: Sigurd and Brynhild are presented as Áslaug’s parents.

Ægir.note: Bragi answers Ægir’s questions about gods, myths, kennings, and poetry.
Freyja accompanies the other deities to Ægir’s feast.
Freyr attends Ægir’s feast, though no direct exchange between them survives.
Gerðr appears among the goddesses attending Ægir’s banquet.
Heimdall participates in Ægir’s feast but does not directly address him.
Loki disrupts Ægir’s feast and abuses Ægir as its host.
Njǫrðr attended Ægir’s feast and participated in its flyting.
Sif attends Ægir’s feast, where she offers Loki mead.
Skaði attends the feast in Ægir’s hall, without directly addressing him.
Thor procures Hymir’s immense cauldron so Ægir can brew ale for the gods.
Tyr helps arrange Ægir’s feast by identifying where a sufficiently large cauldron can be found.
Vidar attends the feast in Ægir’s hall without direct dialogue.

Æsir.note: The einherjar arm and advance alongside the Æsir at Ragnarǫk.
Freyja introduces the Æsir to Vanir seiðr magic.
Iðunn preserves or restores the Æsir’s youth with their rejuvenating remedy.
The Æsir compel Loki’s rescue and kill Þjazi after Iðunn returns.
The Æsir burn or kill Þjazi while he pursues Loki.
The Æsir settle Skaði's claim with husband-choice and laughter.
Surtr leads Muspell's forces against the gods and burns the world.
Ægir and Rán host the gods at divine feasts.
Hyrrokkin launches Baldr's funeral ship when the gods cannot.
The Vanir gave Njǫrðr to the Æsir as a hostage establishing peace.

Æsir.myth: Final battle on Óskópnir or Vígríðr
Æsir.note: Surtr battles the assembled gods and mingles blood with the Æsir.

Æsir.myth: Surtr defeats the gods at Ragnarök
Æsir.note: Surtr defeats the gods before casting fire over the world.

Ívaldi.note: Viktor Rydberg reconstructs Völundr as Ívaldi's son; medieval texts do not.

Ófnir.note: Ófnir and Níðhǫggr are colocated beneath Yggdrasill without further interaction.

Ótr.note: Ótr, whose killing prompts the ransom, is Fáfnir’s brother.
Loki kills an otter that is actually the shape-shifted Ótr.
Odin travels with Hœnir and Loki when Ótr is killed.

Óttarr.note: Freyja obtains ancestry and a memory drink to help her devotee Óttarr.
Hyndla alleges that Freyja’s boar is Óttarr in disguise.

Óðinn.note: Some scholars conjecture Óðinn promised or helped promise the maiden to Alvíss.
Baldr is repeatedly named as Óðinn’s son.
Óðinn rides to Hel and questions a dead seeress about Baldr’s doom.
Óðinn gives Draupnir at the funeral; Baldr later returns it through Hermóðr.
Óðinn whispers unknowable words in Baldr’s ear before the pyre.
Snorri identifies Bragi as Óðinn’s son.
Óðinn questions Bragi about the tumult announcing Eiríkr’s arrival.

Óðinn.myth: Hákon the Good’s reception in Valhǫll
Óðinn.note: Bragi obeys Óðinn’s command to welcome the dead Hákon.
Óðinn strikes Brynhild with a sleep-thorn and condemns her to marriage.
Brynhild invokes or describes Óðinn-associated divine powers while teaching runic lore.
Borr is Óðinn's father; poetic and prose sources together identify the relationship.
Bestla is Óðinn's mother, securely preserved in an early skaldic kenning.
Óðinn awakens and commands the einherjar while preparing Valhǫll for Eiríkr.
Óðinn grants Hákon the einherjar’s peace and directs his reception.
The einherjar fight daily within Óðinn’s enclosures and reconcile afterward.
Óðinn leads the armed einherjar onto Vígríðr against Fenrir’s forces.
Óðinn helps pay the ransom that later becomes Fáfnir’s hoard.
Freyja chooses half the slain each day; Óðinn receives the remainder.
The euhemerized narrative presents Freyja as Óðinn’s concubine.
Óðinn orders Loki to steal Freyja’s necklace and withholds its return.
Óðinn’s divine community receives Freyr as a settlement member or hostage.
Freyr sits on Óðinn’s high seat Hliðskjálf and sees Gerðr.
Freyr sees Gerðr from Óðinn’s seat, and Skírnir offers her Óðinn’s ring.
Óðinn and Gerðr appear as guests in Ægir’s feast-frame.
Óðinn is present when Þjazi forces Loki’s bargain concerning Iðunn.
Óðinn’s sending or questioning of messengers frames Iðunn’s obscure condition.
Óðinn, Vili, and Vé kill Ymir and fashion the cosmos.
Bestla and Bölþorn place Óðinn within a maternal Jotunn lineage.
Bölþorn's unnamed son teaches Óðinn nine mighty songs.
Mímir gives counsel, and Óðinn drinks from his well for an eye.
Vafþrúðnir loses a fatal wisdom contest against the disguised Óðinn.
Gunnlǫð sleeps with Óðinn for three nights and grants three drinks.
Óðinn betrays Gunnlǫð and takes all the guarded mead.
Óðinn steals Suttungr's mead and escapes his eagle-form pursuit.
Óðinn labors for Baugi, who helps bore into Hnitbjörg.
Hrungnir races Sleipnir, enters Ásgarðr, and becomes violently boastful.
Fenrir swallows Óðinn during Ragnarök.
Óðinn casts Hel into Niflheim and grants authority over certain dead.
The giantess Jörð unites with Óðinn and bears Þórr.
Later genealogy makes the Jotunn Gríðr Óðinn's partner and Víðarr's mother.
Loki invokes their mingled blood to compel Óðinn to admit him.
Loki travels with Óðinn and Hœnir during their encounter with Þjazi.
Loki travels with Óðinn and Hœnir and obtains Ótr’s ransom.
Loki and Óðinn trade accusations concerning injustice, sex change, and childbirth.
Loki bears Sleipnir and gives the eight-legged horse to Óðinn.
At Óðinn’s command, Loki steals Freyja’s necklace.
Óðinn appointed Njǫrðr a sacrificial priest within the Æsir community.
Óðinn assigned the estate Nóatún to Njǫrðr.
Njǫrðr succeeded Óðinn as Sweden’s ruler and marked himself for Óðinn before death.
Separate ritual cups honored Óðinn and Njǫrðr during the pagan feast.
Óðinn as Grímnir describes Ratatoskr’s existence and function without meeting him.
Óðinn fathers Sæmingr and other sons with Skaði.
Snorri says Skaði marries Óðinn after rejecting Njǫrðr.
As compensation, Óðinn casts Þjazi’s eyes into heaven as stars.
Sleipnir is Óðinn's eight-legged mount for the ride to Urðarbrunnr.

Óðinn.myth: Óðinn rides to the dead seeress
Óðinn.note: Sleipnir carries Óðinn downward to Niflhel to question a dead seeress.
Sleipnir carries Óðinn ahead of Hrungnir and Gullfaxi into Ásgarðr.
Óðinn riding Sleipnir forms the riddle's ten feet, three eyes, and tail.
Ollerus takes Othinus’s authority and name, then flees when Othinus is restored.
Váli is the son of Óðinn, begotten specifically to avenge Baldr.
Óðinn begets Váli for the explicit purpose of avenging Baldr.
In Saxo’s variant, Bous is the son of Othinus and Rinda.
Othinus orders Bous to attack Balderus’s killer rather than innocent people.
Óðinn sends Gǫndul and Skǫgul to choose Hákon and announce his arrival.
Óðinn dispatches Valkyries to battles, where they determine death and victory.
Gunnr, Róta, and Skuld ride at Óðinn’s command to govern fighting.
Óðinn gives Sigrdrífa a sleep-thorn after she grants victory against his will.
Sigrún attributes Helgi’s spirit or victory-related destiny indirectly to Óðinn.

Óðr.note: Óðr is Freyja’s husband and father of her daughters.
Freyja searches foreign lands for absent Óðr and weeps red gold.

Ölvaldi.note: Ölvaldi is Skaði’s paternal grandfather through his son Þjazi.

Úlfrún.note: Úlfrún is one of the nine giant sisters who bore Heimdall.

Útgarða-Loki.myth: The cat contest at Útgarða-Loki’s hall
Útgarða-Loki.note: Útgarða-Loki presents Jǫrmungandr deceptively as a cat for Thor to lift.
Loki competes in Útgarða-Loki’s hall; the narrative treats them as separate beings.
Útgarða-Loki humiliates Thor with illusions involving sea, serpent, and Old Age.

Þjazi.note: Þjazi is an unspecified kinsman of Gerðr’s family.
Þjazi obtains Iðunn through Loki’s betrayal, depriving the gods of rejuvenation.
Þjazi carries Iðunn to Þrymheimr, confines her, and pursues her rescuer.
Loki strikes eagle-shaped Þjazi with a pole and is dragged through the air.
Coerced by Þjazi, Loki promises and delivers Iðunn outside Ásgarðr.
Loki infiltrates Þjazi’s home and escapes with Iðunn transformed into a nut.
Loki boasts to Skaði that he was foremost in causing Þjazi’s death.
Skaði is consistently identified as Þjazi’s daughter and heir.
She arms herself and demands compensation from the gods after Þjazi’s death.

Þjálfi.note: Þjálfi kills Hrungnir's clay helper Mǫkkurkálfi.
Útgarða-Loki matches Þjálfi's speed against Hugi, personified thought.
Þjálfi becomes Thor’s servant after breaking a resurrected goat’s bone.
Þjálfi assists Thor by tricking Hrungnir and defeating the clay giant.

Þrymr.note: Þrymr demands Freyja as his bride in exchange for Mjǫllnir.
Disguised as a maid, Loki helps conceal bridal Þórr’s identity from Þrymr.
Þrymr steals Thor’s hammer and demands Freyja as its ransom.
Thor disguises himself as Þrymr’s bride to regain Mjǫllnir.
Thor recovers Mjǫllnir and kills Þrymr.

Þrymr’s sister.note: Thor kills Þrymr’s unnamed sister after she requests bridal gifts.

Þræll.note: As Rígr, Heimdall fathers Þræll, ancestor of enslaved laborers.

Þrúðgelmir.note: Aurgelmir is named as Þrúðgelmir's father.

Þrúðr.note: Later tradition identifies Þórr’s unnamed promised maiden as Þrúðr, though no marriage occurs.
Þrúðr bears ale to the einherjar.
Snorri makes Þrúðr the daughter of Sif and Þórr.
Þrúðr is Thor’s daughter; her maternity is not consistently explicit.

Þórr.note: Þórr tests Alvíss with thirteen questions about names used across worlds.
Þórr feigns conditional consent and prolongs questioning until daylight catches Alvíss.
Þórr rejects Alvíss as bridegroom and traps him above ground at dawn.
Þórr kills Hrungnir but is pinned and wounded by whetstone.
Þrymr steals Mjǫllnir and demands Freyja as its ransom.
Disguised as a bride, Þórr recovers Mjǫllnir and kills Þrymr.
Hymir tests Þórr with cups, oxen, fishing, and the cauldron.
Hymir and pursuing giants fight Þórr after he takes the cauldron.
Þórr kills Geirröðr with a red-hot iron projectile.
Gríðr warns Þórr and lends him staff, belt, and gloves.
Gjálp swells the river against Þórr, who later breaks her back.
Greip and Gjálp try crushing Þórr; he breaks their backs.
Útgarða-Loki humiliates Þórr with contests concealed by cosmic illusions.
Elli, personified Old Age, wrestles Þórr to one knee.
Þórr hooks and strikes Jörmungandr during the fishing expedition.
Jörmungandr kills Þórr with venom after receiving a fatal blow.
Þórr kills Jörmungandr before dying from its venom.
Þórr nearly kills Hyrrokkin after she launches Baldr's ship.
Járnsaxa bears Þórr's son Magni.
Jörð, classified as a giantess, is Þórr's mother.
Þórr kills the unnamed builder after his Jotunn nature is revealed.
Loki induces Þórr to visit Geirrøðr without his hammer or strength-belt.
Loki accompanies Þórr to Útgarðr and participates in the deceptive contests.
Loki discovers Þrymr’s terms and assists bridal-disguised Þórr as his maid.
Þórr repeatedly threatens Loki with Mjǫllnir until Loki leaves.
Ullr is Þórr’s stepson, a relationship preserved in skaldic kennings and Snorri.

Þökk.note: Þökk’s refusal fulfills Hel’s condition for retaining Baldr.
The Æsir believe Loki assumed the giantess Þökk’s identity to withhold tears.
